messages.body_plain:
Based on the PV_Q1 resp. PV_Q1* idea from Chalmers and Ng (2017), I wish to employ a combination of several mirt functions to calculate M2 in the presence of massive missing data by design. I was wondering if anyone had tried the following systematically or can advise on potential pitfalls:

0. Fit preferred IRT model

For k replications (say k = 30):

1. Use fscores to obtain PV estimates Theta
2. Pass on Theta to M2 and impute once. Record M2, RMSEA, ....

3. After the k replications, pool the M2 values etc...

So if my intuition is correct, that might be a (slight?) improvement beyond something like M2(fit, impute = 30), as the uncertainty in the person parameters is more explicitly incorporated by step 1.

What are your thoughts?

messages.subject: Re: Variant of Chalmers & Ng (2017) procedure for M2
messages.subject_clean: Variant of Chalmers & Ng (2017) procedure for M2
messages.body_plain:
It would be a slight improvement, but the problem will be the implicit imputation based on assuming the correct model has been specified. The plausible value draws don't account for that property explicitly, though you're correct there will be more response variability than using point estimates and so should be more conservative. In situations like these, with massive amounts of missing data, it is often better to included independent information for the imputation task (re: multiple imputation methods) so to avoid 'double-dipping' the data. Otherwise, you could go about this plausible value imputation technique, but would have to approximate the null distribution in a way similar to the PV_Q1* approach.... which for the M2 statistic, could take up an unreasonable amount of computer resources.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
Fitting the unconditional GRM is a good starting point, at the very least to determine if the measurement model itself works well. And it sounds as though the bifactor model is the model of choice, so you probably want to reflect this model structure in mixedmirt() as well by constructing a suitable model syntax definition to reflect this structure.

Regarding the C2 statistic, it was noted that the CRAN version was slightly off in version 1.29, so the results may not be overly reliable (though the previous results appeared to be more conservative, so a misfitting model is likely the correct decision anyway. But if you feel like checking, feel free to install the Github dev version yourself). The fit from C2 should be nearly identical to the results you get when fitting similar models with SEM via the WLSMV algorithm for ordered categorical items. HTH.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
W.r.t. to Gene's orginal question on reverse coding: As mirt does not restrict the sign of discrimination parameters, the fit does not change by reverse coding in an uncondtional GRM:

data1 <- simdata(rep(1,5), matrix(2:(-2),ncol = 5, nrow = 5, byrow = TRUE), 500, rep('graded',5))
# reverse first item in data set 2
data2 <- data1
data2[,1] <- 6 - data2[,1] # same number of categories as before with reversed order of labels
fit1 <- mirt(data1,1,itemtype = "graded")
fit2 <- mirt(data2,1,itemtype = "graded")
# identical fit in terms of AIC/BIC etc...

The number of iterations might change (starting values maybe biased towards discrimination parameters with identical resp. positive sign), so if discrepancies in fit occur after reverse coding, convergence problems could be a reason.

Also, local independence should not be violated, if person level covariates are used: After all, one conditions on realizations of random effects (=person parameters) anyway when discussing local independence, so I do not see a problem.

Best,
  Philipp

> So I can’t factor analyze in a classical way because I don’t have the full inter-correaltion of items
>

Correct. mirt uses a full information estimator, so the pairwise patterns do not matter. So long as the missing data are missing at random, which they are by design here, then your estimates will be valid.

>  Are these loadings affected by the structure of the booklets? Are these loadings interpretable ?

No, they are not affected. Loadings have the same interpretation as always.

> Are they similar to what I wold see if I had full test to all subjects and had a full intercorrelation matrix ?

Yes, again, FIML estimator.

> I guess you only  analyze covariance between items that you have concomitant data on response vectors right ?

I suppose so, but that sounds like you may be asking a different question. Regardless, FIML estimators make no assumption about the uni/bi/tri/.... variate correlations since all components are computed row-wise for each unique observation in isolation.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
I don't think the BL method is giving the 'right' answer, actually, especially given that it's reporting so many warning messages (this algorithm implementation is less tested than the EM). Consider the following syntax comparisons using the more stable nlminb optimizer, which works better in more difficult to estimate situations (at the consequence of being notably slower):

set.seed(1)
mod0 <- mirt(dat, model1, optimizer='nlminb', GenRandomPars = TRUE)
mod1 <- mirt(dat, model1, optimizer='nlminb', GenRandomPars = TRUE)
coef(mod0, simplify=TRUE)
coef(mod1, simplify=TRUE)

## above gives the same output

set.seed(1)
mod2 <- mirt(dat, model1, method = 'BL', GenRandomPars = TRUE)
mod3 <- mirt(dat, model1, method = 'BL', GenRandomPars = TRUE)
coef(mod2, simplify=TRUE)
coef(mod3, simplify=TRUE)

## these outputs dramatically differ

The BL method is more than likely terminating early in an unexpected way, and you're simply seeing the last iteration of the parameters right before the algorithm is forced to stop (likely because the correlation becomes something greater than 1).

Phil

messages.subject: Controlling for difficulty with MIRT
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,
     I am hoping to control for item difficulty (literally how difficult/complex) the items are using MIRT. Study design is that:
We have three tests for one group of people (Math test, English test, science test; of 51 items each).
We would like to equate these tests to be the same level of difficulty for that population.
We then wish to administer the three tests to another group of people to see whether the new population is better at all three tasks, or only different on one task, i.e. are they only better at math than the first group, or better at all tests equally.
We hypothesize that the second group should be better with difficulty / more complex questions generally, and that the nature of the test should not matter. Therefore, we want to equating the difficulty/complexity of the questions of the three tests first, to ensure any change in scores is related to actual differences in math/science/English, and not simply a better capacity to handle more complex items.
   The best approach would be to simply run DTF between groups for each exam separately and compare the size of the DIF. However, the second group will only be around 60 people which probably makes the sample size for this group too small for the DTF parameters we want to estimate.

    Would this form of equating be possible in MIRT? I am concerned that the common underlying Theta might not be simply item difficulty, there might be issues then with finding the 4-item anchor, and that we might not achieve unidimensionality assumption. I was also wondering if this were possible in MIRT, what would the size of the calibration sample need to be?

Kind Regards and thanks in advance,
          Conal

messages.subject_clean: Selecting anchor items when using DIF
messages.body_plain:
This is a good question, and one worth investigating via research. In general, anchors must be selected based on a priori invariant items for them to work, where the theoretical minimum number of parameters to constrain is at least 1 slope and one intercept (though clearly that's not the most optimal idea), and the stability of the IRT model also makes a difference. More anchors the better, but of course this requires stronger prior knowledge as well. There have been algorithmic approaches to try and solve this problem based on alternative selection criteria (e.g., see the work by Carol Woods), but I'm not completely sure how much I trust these algorithms just yet without testing them myself.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Controlling for difficulty with MIRT
messages.body_plain:
Hi Conal,

On Thu, Oct 25, 2018 at 7:28 PM Conal Monaghan <conal.m...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi All,
>      I am hoping to control for item difficulty (literally how difficult/complex) the items are using MIRT. Study design is that:
> We have three tests for one group of people (Math test, English test, science test; of 51 items each).
> We would like to equate these tests to be the same level of difficulty for that population.

You lost me here. If you have distinct constructs then how could you equate them to have similar properties? Equating has to do with matching distributions from the same random effect (the latent traits), which generally occurs in multiple-group settings where individuals take overlapping items (sometimes completely overlapping, where the groups end up taking the exactly the same test items). At best, it sounds like you should be fitting independent unidimensional IRT models and selecting items with similar properties (e.g., similar slopes and intercepts, likely between a desired range).

> We then wish to administer the three tests to another group of people to see whether the new population is better at all three tasks, or only different on one task, i.e. are they only better at math than the first group, or better at all tests equally.

This is where the multiple-group equating comes in. In which case you are really looking at a constrained (all latent hyper parameters equal) versus unconstrained (freeing the hyper parameters in the new group) to determine if the more free model 'fits the data better' (e.g., rejecting the null hypothesis of equal trait properties via something like a likelihood-ratio test).

> We hypothesize that the second group should be better with difficulty / more complex questions generally, and that the nature of the test should not matter. Therefore, we want to equating the difficulty/complexity of the questions of the three tests first, to ensure any change in scores is related to actual differences in math/science/English, and not simply a better capacity to handle more complex items.
>    The best approach would be to simply run DTF between groups for each exam separately and compare the size of the DIF. However, the second group will only be around 60 people which probably makes the sample size for this group too small for the DTF parameters we want to estimate.

DIF() seems to be what you are after, run three times for each isolated testing instrument. I would recommend the new DRF() function though to quantify the magnitude of the DIF, and if you are interested in DTF effects. There's a related paper in that function documentation explaining why the DRF statistics are superior to most (if not all available) measures of effect size in bias studies.

>
>     Would this form of equating be possible in MIRT? I am concerned that the common underlying Theta might not be simply item difficulty, there might be issues then with finding the 4-item anchor, and that we might not achieve unidimensionality assumption. I was also wondering if this were possible in MIRT, what would the size of the calibration sample need to be?

The results would still be fine if you did run three separate unidimensional models, so I would start with those first for simplicity reasons.

>

> Kind Regards and thanks in advance,
>           Conal
